noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: practical: investigate how enzyme activity can be affected by changes in pH

primer.text: The pH version of the amylase practical swaps the water bath for buffer solutions at pH 3, 5, 7, 9 and 11, with iodine wells still acting as the clock. This note walks the method, the safety list, the reading of results around the optimum, and the CORMS plan, finishing with the warning that any pH outside the optimum can denature the enzyme.

lessons.title: Buffers, droplets and the pH clock
lessons.opening: Buffer solutions hold each tube at a fixed pH while amylase attacks starch. Every ten seconds a droplet moves to a fresh iodine well, and the run ends the first time the yellow-brown colour survives. The buffer at pH 3 starts the sweep, with repeats at 5, 7, 9 and 11 building the comparison across the pH scale.
keyPoints: Buffer solutions at different pH values hold each tube's conditions constant.
Amylase and buffer are mixed, then starch is added and the stopwatch starts.
A droplet transfers to a fresh iodine well every ten seconds until blue-black stops appearing.
The run is repeated with buffers at pH values such as 5, 7, 9 and 11.
Iodine and amylase irritate eyes, so goggles are worn, and gloves guard against amylase on skin.

low.restatement: Mix amylase with a pH buffer, add starch, time it: droplet to a fresh iodine well every ten seconds; count wells until the blue-black stops. Repeat across pH 3 to 11.
low.analogy: The buffer is a thermostat for acidity: it clamps the pH so only the pH you chose is being tested.
low.examPointer: State the interval (every 10 seconds) — the pH practical's timing differs from the temperature version's minute intervals.

medium.restatement: Buffers convert pH from an uncontrolled nuisance into the independent variable; the well count then gives each pH a comparable digestion time, and the shortest count locates the optimum.
medium.analogy: Each buffer tube is one lane of a swimming gala held at a different water temperature — the lane clocks are only comparable because the lanes differ in exactly one thing.
medium.examPointer: Name goggles AND gloves in safety answers — the note assigns eye irritation to goggles and skin irritation to gloves.

check.stem: What is the job of the buffer solutions in this practical?

options.text: To hold each tube at a fixed, chosen pH
options.explanation: Buffers clamp the pH as the independent variable.

options.text: To digest the starch directly
options.explanation: Amylase does the digesting.

options.text: To colour the solution blue-black
options.explanation: Iodine provides the colour.

options.text: To warm the tubes
options.explanation: Temperature is controlled separately.

check.stem: How often is a droplet transferred to a fresh iodine well?

options.text: Every time the colour changes
options.explanation: Transfers are on a fixed schedule.

options.text: Every ten seconds
options.explanation: The pH practical uses ten-second transfers.

options.text: Every ten minutes
options.explanation: Far too slow for the reaction.

options.text: Only once at the end
options.explanation: The series of transfers IS the timing.

check.stem: What marks the end of a digestion run at one pH on the iodine tile?

options.text: The stopwatch reaching one minute
options.explanation: Runs end on the colour, not a fixed time.

options.text: The buffer changing colour
options.explanation: Buffers do not change colour.

options.text: The first iodine well that stays yellow-brown
options.explanation: No blue-black means no starch left.

options.text: The first well that turns blue-black
options.explanation: That is the START of the story.

check.stem: Which safety pairing of goggles and gloves matches the note?

options.text: Gloves for eye protection; goggles for skin
options.explanation: The protections are swapped.

options.text: No protection needed
options.explanation: Both hazards are named.

options.text: Goggles only for the buffers
options.explanation: The hazards are the solutions, not the buffers.

options.text: Goggles for eye irritation from iodine and amylase; gloves for amylase on skin
options.explanation: Both protections map to their named hazards.

check.stem: Why is the same volume of amylase used at every pH?

options.text: So that only pH differs between tubes and the comparison stays fair
options.explanation: Equal enzyme concentration is the CORMS control.

options.text: Because amylase is expensive
options.explanation: Cost is not the design reason.

options.text: Because amylase changes pH otherwise
options.explanation: Amylase does not set the pH.

options.text: Because buffers would react with more amylase
options.explanation: No such reaction is claimed.

check.stem: Name the enzyme whose activity is tested across pH values here.
State the pH values the note suggests sweeping across.
Explain why a fresh iodine well is needed for every ten-second droplet.
check.modelAnswer: Each well's iodine reacts with the starch in the droplet it receives and cannot report again, so a fresh well per droplet keeps every ten-second reading independent and lets the well count act as a clock.

check.stem: A run at pH 9 stops changing colour after 6 wells while pH 7 stops after 3. Which pH sits nearer amylase's optimum, and what would you expect at pH 11?
check.modelAnswer: pH 7 is nearer the optimum because its shorter well count means faster digestion; at pH 11 the count should lengthen again as the strongly alkaline conditions denature more enzyme, mirroring the far-acid behaviour at pH 3.

lessons.title: Reading the pH curve and planning with CORMS
lessons.opening: Results read the same way as the temperature practical: the shortest well count marks the optimum pH, where iodine quit blue-black fastest, and counts lengthen on both sides as denaturation bites. CORMS then assembles the plan — change the pH, hold the enzyme concentration, repeat, measure via wells, and fix the temperature and volumes.
keyPoints: At the optimum pH the iodine stops turning blue-black in the shortest time.
Above or below the optimum the count stretches because the enzyme is losing shape.
Denaturation on either side of the optimum prevents the substrate binding the active site.
The CORMS plan changes pH, holds enzyme concentration, repeats, measures by wells, and controls temperature and volumes.

low.restatement: Shortest count = optimum pH. Counts grow away from it because the enzyme denatures and binds less substrate.
low.analogy: The pH curve is a valley: the enzyme works at the valley floor and stumbles on both slopes.
low.examPointer: Say 'both sides' when explaining the pattern — one-sided answers lose the symmetry mark.

medium.restatement: The pH curve's symmetry comes from one mechanism acting twice: ion-driven shape loss near either end of the scale reduces effective enzyme concentration, stretching every well count away from the optimum.
medium.analogy: Denaturation is a tax charged on both sides of the optimum; the further you trade from the peak, the higher the rate you pay.
medium.examPointer: Any pH outside the optimum can denature the enzyme — the note's closing hint makes that sentence worth writing verbatim in spirit.

check.stem: What does the shortest well count identify?

options.text: The optimum pH for amylase in this experiment
options.explanation: Fastest digestion locates the optimum.

options.text: The most alkaline buffer used
options.explanation: Alkalinity is not the readout.

options.text: The tube with the most starch
options.explanation: Starch volumes are controlled.

options.text: The temperature of the room
options.explanation: Temperature is controlled, not measured here.

check.stem: Why do well counts lengthen on BOTH sides of the optimum?

options.text: Because buffers thicken at extremes
options.explanation: No thickening is claimed.

options.text: Because denaturation away from the optimum reduces the enzyme's working shape either way
options.explanation: One mechanism, two directions.

options.text: Because starch dissolves better at extremes
options.explanation: Starch solubility is not the mechanism.

options.text: Because iodine reacts faster at extremes
options.explanation: Iodine behaviour does not change.

check.stem: Which CORMS element corresponds to holding the enzyme concentration constant?

options.text: The O — organism
options.explanation: O covers the organism or enzyme source.

options.text: The M — measure
options.explanation: M is the well count.

options.text: The S — same or controlled variables
options.explanation: Enzyme concentration sits in the control list.

options.text: The C — change
options.explanation: C is pH, the thing varied.

check.stem: What happens to amylase's activity at pH values far from its optimum?

options.text: It rises because the enzyme stretches out
options.explanation: Stretching destroys fit.

options.text: It stays the same
options.explanation: The curve's slopes deny this.

options.text: It becomes measurable only with a colorimeter
options.explanation: Activity change is measurable by wells.

options.text: It falls because the active site is denatured and the substrate cannot bind
options.explanation: The binding-loss pathway is the answer.

check.stem: A graph of pH against rate for a duodenum enzyme peaks around pH 8. Which statement follows?

options.text: The enzyme's optimum is mildly alkaline, matching its small-intestine home
options.explanation: Peak location = optimum, and the duodenum is alkaline.

options.text: The enzyme works best in strong acid
options.explanation: The peak is alkaline.

options.text: The enzyme denatures at its peak
options.explanation: The peak is where it works BEST.

options.text: The graph says nothing about optimum
options.explanation: Peak position is exactly the optimum.

check.stem: State the reading that marks the optimum pH in this practical.
check.modelAnswer: The shortest well count at which iodine no longer turns blue-black.

check.stem: Name the process that reduces activity on either side of the optimum pH.
Explain why the same amylase can show a shortest count at pH 7 in class even though some commercial amylase preparations peak elsewhere.
check.modelAnswer: Optimum pH tracks the conditions an enzyme is produced for and the exact preparation used, so class results locate the optimum of THIS amylase sample; a different source or a duodenum enzyme can carry a different peak without contradicting the method.

check.stem: A technician must redesign this practical to test pH 4 only, with all else fixed. Using CORMS, state the C, the M and one S.
check.modelAnswer: C: change the pH to 4 (against the comparison runs); M: measure the time by counting ten-second wells until iodine stays yellow-brown; S: same amylase concentration, starch volume and temperature across tubes.

glossary.definition: A solution that holds pH constant, letting one pH value be tested per tube.
The pH where amylase digests starch fastest, shown by the shortest well count.
To permanently lose an enzyme's working shape, preventing substrate binding.
